entries.clue: Collect label returned by that woman (6)

indicatorNotes.returned: Returned means sent back the way it came, so the word before it is read from its far end — and in an across entry that is right to left.

blocks.note: a label tied to a parcel is a tag, and the instruction turns those three letters round
her is how you refer to a woman once she has been pointed at

annotation.surface: A luggage tag sent back by a woman, and somebody picking it up.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one unbroken sentence about a parcel, which is what hides the seam after its first word. Her, him and his are the crossword's standing handovers for that woman and that man.
annotation.definitionFit: To gather up belongings is to collect them, the same act of bringing scattered things together in one place.

entries.clue: Extreme neatness as taken at a patisserie? (5-3,5)

annotation.definition: Extreme neatness as taken at a patisserie?

blocks.note: the state the phrase names: everything squared away, nothing left out of place
a French pastry shop takes requests across its counter, and one word covers both that request and the tidiness above

annotation.surface: Choosing something from the counter of a French pastry shop.
annotation.walkthrough: There is nothing here to take apart into letters; the phrase simply does two jobs at once, and the question mark is the setter admitting it. The 5-3 enumeration is the strongest mechanical hint, since very little English is written with a hyphen in that spot.
annotation.definitionFit: Apple-pie order is the set English phrase for perfect tidiness, and the joke is that a patisserie counter really would take an order for apple pie.

entries.clue: Locks security device? (7)

blocks.note: locks is what a shampoo advertisement calls the stuff growing on your head
a net is what goes over a thing to stop it getting away — over a load on a lorry, under a trapeze

annotation.surface: A gadget fitted to the locks on a door to keep it shut.
annotation.walkthrough: Locks is the pivot: a door has them and so does a head of hair, and only one of those ever needs holding in place. The clue defines its answer and spells it out in the same three words, which is the rarest shape in cryptics.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight: a hairnet is the device that keeps a head of locks secure, and its two halves say so a piece at a time.

entries.clue: System for Reg and I to go ahead of troops (7)

indicatorNotes.to go ahead of: To go ahead of something is to take the place in front of it, so the pieces just named are written down before the one that follows — in a down entry, in the rows above it.

blocks.note: the shortened first name, taken down exactly as it is spelt
the single letter anybody speaking calls themselves
troops are the men in the ranks, the ordinary soldiers

annotation.surface: Reg and the speaker being let march at the front of the column.
annotation.walkthrough: Reg looks like half a name because that is all the clue wants — spelt out whole, not abbreviated. Regiment is the near-miss the soldiering surface is steering you towards, and the enumeration is one letter short of it.
annotation.definitionFit: A regimen is the fixed routine of diet, exercise or treatment somebody is put on, which is a system for living by.

entries.clue: Traces changes, as responds to stimulus (6)

indicatorNotes.changes: Something that changes does not stay as it was, and letters that do not stay as they were are letters standing in a new order.

blocks.note: the six letters of the clue's first word, set down in a different order

annotation.surface: Faint marks shifting about the moment something is prodded.
annotation.walkthrough: Traces sits at the head of the clue looking like a verb, which is the disguise: it is six letters waiting to be rearranged. The comma is all that separates the instruction from the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: To react is to answer something acting on you — heat, light, an insult — which is what responding to a stimulus means.

entries.clue: Some explorer unnecessarily has to go again (5)

indicatorNotes.Some: Some asks for a part of what follows rather than all of it, and that part is already spelt out there without a letter moved.

blocks.note: five letters in an unbroken run that carries on across the gap between the two words

annotation.surface: An explorer going back over old ground for no good reason.
annotation.walkthrough: Concealments hide best across a space between two long words, because neither word looks short of business. Unnecessarily earns its keep twice: it holds up the surface and lends the tail of the run.
annotation.definitionFit: To rerun a race or a television programme is to put it through a second time, which is to go again.

entries.clue: Sacrificial block to change, we hear (5)

indicatorNotes.we hear: We hear says the words before it reach you as a noise rather than as spelling, so it is the sound that has to be written down.

blocks.note: to change something is to alter it, and that word said aloud can be written a second way

annotation.surface: Being told that a stone slab is due to be altered.
annotation.walkthrough: English keeps two spellings for this one noise and gives them entirely unrelated jobs, one a verb of change and one a piece of temple furniture. Only the crossing letters say which spelling the grid is holding out for.
annotation.definitionFit: An altar is the raised stone table a temple kills its offerings on, so a sacrificial block names it plainly.

entries.clue: Phew! Be grateful to my following! (5,8)

indicatorNotes.following: Following means coming along behind, so the piece it names is set down after the one already in hand — in a down entry, in the squares underneath.

blocks.note: to be grateful to somebody out loud is to thank them
my! on its own is a mild cry of surprise, and there is a longer word that does exactly the same job

annotation.surface: Somebody demanding gratitude from the people who follow them.
annotation.walkthrough: My and goodness are each an exclamation of surprise in their own right, which is what lets one stand in for the other. The exclamation marks are surface decoration; underneath, this is a plain two-part charade.
annotation.definitionFit: Phew is the breath of relief let out when something has just been dodged, and thank goodness is that same relief put into words.

entries.clue: Jumper for a spaniel? (8)

blocks.note: one that springs, taking the verb and adding the ordinary ending for a doer
one particular breed of the dog, and the question mark marks it as an example rather than a synonym

annotation.surface: A woolly pullover knitted to fit a dog.
annotation.walkthrough: Jumper wants to be a garment, and the surface never gives you a reason to doubt it. The breed is named for the job it did on a shoot: springing game birds out of the undergrowth for the guns.
annotation.definitionFit: A springer is anything that springs, which is a jumper, and a springer spaniel is one named breed of spaniel — a definition by example, hence the question mark.

entries.clue: Holder is very French, it's said (4)

indicatorNotes.it's said: It's said means the words before it are to be heard rather than read, so what counts is their noise and not the way they are spelt.

blocks.note: très is French for very, and its ending comes out of an English mouth as the vowel in 'say'

annotation.surface: A container being described as thoroughly French.
annotation.walkthrough: Holder is deliberately vague — a box, a rack, a stand would all fit the word — so the four letters have to come from the sound. Snippets of French are fair game in a British cryptic and très is the commonest of them.
annotation.definitionFit: A tray is the flat thing with a lip round its edge that a waiter carries drinks on, a holder for whatever is set down on it.

entries.clue: Felled when agitated (4)

indicatorNotes.agitated: Something agitated has been shaken about, and letters shaken about do not come to rest in the order they started in.

blocks.note: the four letters of the middle word, resettled in another order

annotation.surface: Somebody knocked flat in the middle of losing their temper.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words, and the middle one is the whole of the fodder — the shortest possible anagram clue. Hewn is the old past participle of hew, the verb for cutting timber down with an axe.
annotation.definitionFit: To hew a tree is to cut it down, so timber that has been hewn has been felled.

entries.clue: Male sailor finds poisonous plant (8)

blocks.note: the plainest word for a male human being
Sir Francis Drake sailed round the world for Elizabeth I and is the crossword's standing seaman

annotation.surface: A seaman coming across something deadly growing.
annotation.walkthrough: No word here means a mariner in general; the clue wants one particular Elizabethan by name, which is a habit worth learning early. Finds is joinery, the verb that lets the sentence stand up.
annotation.definitionFit: The mandrake is a poisonous member of the nightshade family whose forked root looks like a little man, which is where its folklore comes from.

entries.clue: Practically besotted by hand warmer (6)

indicatorNotes.Practically: Practically means all but a scrap of the word beside it; the clue does not say which end the scrap comes off, and only one of the two choices leaves a word behind.

blocks.note: somebody smitten with another person is besotted with them
the one letter left off, the scrap that stops it being the whole word

annotation.surface: Being nearly in love with the thing that keeps your hand warm.
annotation.walkthrough: Practically normally trims the tail off a word and here it takes the head instead, so the crossing letters are what settle the reading. Hand warmer is one noun written in two words, not a person who warms hands.
annotation.definitionFit: A mitten is the glove with no separate fingers, made for keeping a hand warm rather than for doing anything fiddly.

entries.clue: Points out engine part (6)

indicatorNotes.out: Out here means out of its proper arrangement, so the letters beside it are to be set down in some other order.

blocks.note: the six letters of the first word, rearranged

annotation.surface: Somebody indicating a component under the bonnet.
annotation.walkthrough: Points out reads as an ordinary verb, which is exactly why the first word slips past as fodder. Setters love out in this job because it does its surface work and its instruction with the same three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A piston is the plug that slides up and down inside an engine's cylinder, pushed by the burning fuel — an engine part in the most literal sense.

entries.clue: Vegetable, the average bargain (7)

blocks.note: par is the standard a golfer is measured against, and to be on par with something is to be level with the ordinary run of it
a snip is British for something going far cheaper than it ought to — a snip at thirty quid

annotation.surface: A vegetable said to be no better than an ordinary bargain.
annotation.walkthrough: The comma does all the joining this clue needs, so both halves of the wordplay sit bare after it. Average and bargain are both everyday words hiding shorter everyday words.
annotation.definitionFit: The parsnip is the pale tapering root that goes into the roasting tin beside the potatoes.

entries.clue: Realist, when surreal, is more like the sea (7)

indicatorNotes.surreal: Surreal things are the ordinary set out in an arrangement it never comes in, which is what has to happen to the letters beside it.

blocks.note: the seven letters of the clue's first word, put down in another order

annotation.surface: A down-to-earth person turning dreamlike.
annotation.walkthrough: Realist and surreal are near-opposites, which is what holds the sentence together while one of them shuffles the other. Seawater is salt water, so the comparison being made is with the sea itself, not with a salty taste.
annotation.definitionFit: The sea is salt water, so the more salt a thing carries the closer it comes to being sea.

entries.clue: Tore robe off, given drink in America (4,4)

indicatorNotes.off: Something off has gone bad or gone wrong, and letters that have gone wrong are letters no longer standing where they should.

blocks.note: the eight letters of the first two words, redealt into two new ones

annotation.surface: Stripping a gown off after being handed a drink in the States.
annotation.walkthrough: Eight letters sit in the clue's first two words and the enumeration splits them four and four, which is the pairing to test before anything else. Off does its instruction job while the surface reads it as undressing.
annotation.definitionFit: Root beer is the sweet sarsaparilla-flavoured soft drink sold on every American street corner and almost nowhere in Britain.

entries.clue: Peg points to adolescents (5)

blocks.note: the little spike a golfer sets the ball on before driving off
north and south, two of the four points a compass names, each written as its initial

annotation.surface: Somebody called Peg gesturing towards a group of youngsters.
annotation.walkthrough: Peg is a woman's name in the surface and a golfer's plastic spike in the wordplay. Compass points are the crossword's most reliable source of single letters, and this clue wants two of them at once.
annotation.definitionFit: The teens are the years from thirteen to nineteen, and the people living through them — adolescents.

entries.clue: Recall last part of remnant (5)

indicatorNotes.last part of: The last part of a word is the run of letters at its tail, so the opening ones are left behind and only the end is written down.

blocks.note: to recall something is to remember it, and it is the eight letters of that longer verb the clue wants in hand

annotation.surface: Casting your mind back over the tail end of a leftover scrap.
annotation.walkthrough: Recall looks like the definition sitting where definitions usually sit; it is the raw material, and the word at the far end is doing the defining instead. Five letters come off the back of an eight-letter verb and stand on their own.
annotation.definitionFit: An ember is the glowing fragment left when a fire has burnt down, which is what remains of it — a remnant.

entries.clue: Title Gladys holds (4)

indicatorNotes.holds: To hold something is to have it inside you, so the word beside this already contains what is wanted, spelt out and unbroken.

blocks.note: four letters in a row inside the name, one letter in from each end

annotation.surface: A woman named Gladys who has a title to her name.
annotation.walkthrough: Holds is both the concealment marker and a natural verb for somebody possessing a title, which is why the name goes unexamined. A six-letter word with a four-letter answer inside leaves only three places to start.
annotation.definitionFit: Lady is the title borne by a peer's wife or by a knight's — Lady Macbeth, Lady Thatcher — and it goes in front of the name.

entries.clue: Unemployed star, they say (4)

indicatorNotes.they say: They say means the word before it is being spoken rather than spelt, so it is wanted for its noise.

blocks.note: a star is an idol, the one everybody worships, and that word said aloud can be written a second way

annotation.surface: A celebrity reportedly out of work.
annotation.walkthrough: One noise, two spellings, and the surface hands you the wrong one — an out-of-work star is a believable sentence all by itself. They say is the only thing telling you to listen instead of read.
annotation.definitionFit: Somebody idle has nothing on — idle hands, an idle machine, an idle workforce — so the word covers being out of work.

entries.clue: Burning garden features, black ones surrounding tree (8)

indicatorNotes.surrounding: What surrounds a thing closes round it on both sides, so the word before this opens up and lets the one named after sit inside it.

blocks.note: B is black on a pencil and on a chessboard
the word itself, taken down whole and then prised apart
a fir is the evergreen with needles, three letters long and a crossword staple

annotation.surface: A gardener pointing out the dark shapes standing round a tree.
annotation.walkthrough: Ones is the sort of word a solver's eye skates over, and here it is the container doing most of the work. Black ones reads as a description of things in the garden and is really two separate instructions.
annotation.definitionFit: A bonfire is the heap of garden waste set alight after an afternoon's clearing — burning, and as much a garden fixture as the compost heap.

entries.clue: Rubber ring opens, but remove first (6)

indicatorNotes.opens: What opens a word is the letter standing at its very front, so that single letter is all this takes.
indicatorNotes.first: First is an instruction about placing rather than about letters: the piece it names goes at the head of the answer, ahead of the one mentioned earlier.

blocks.note: to remove a word from a page is to erase it
the letter that opens the word ring

annotation.surface: A rubber ring splitting open, with something to be taken off before anything else.
annotation.walkthrough: Rubber ring is a real object and the clue banks on you reading the two words as a pair; only the first of them is the definition. First and opens look like the same sort of word and are not — one places a chunk, the other picks a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: A rubber is what a British school calls the thing on the end of a pencil, and an eraser is the same object under its other name.

entries.clue: Seraph's strange group of words (6)

indicatorNotes.strange: Something strange is not as it ought to be, and letters that are not as they ought to be are letters out of their proper order.

blocks.note: the six letters of the angel's name, dealt out again in a different order

annotation.surface: An angel with an oddly worded turn of speech.
annotation.walkthrough: A six-letter word at the head of the clue and a six-letter answer is the shape to check first. The possessive 's is doing nothing but holding the sentence together.
annotation.definitionFit: A phrase is a short run of words handled as a single unit — in the nick of time, by and large — smaller than a sentence.
